title: New York Declares Measles Disaster Emergency as Rural Outbreak Spreads to 18 Counties
excerpt: Governor Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency on October 5 after 108 measles cases this year, expanding who can test and vaccinate as the US endures its worst measles year since 1991.
body:
• Governor Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency on October 5 after New York reported 108 measles cases this year through October 3, according to Reuters.
  • Ninety-two cases have come since July 15, clustered in under-immunized rural communities across 18 counties; seven cases are in New York City and 101 elsewhere in the state.
  • The order lets registered nurses order measles tests and pharmacists vaccinate children as young as two, and requires all MMR shots to be reported to state or city immunization registries within 72 hours.
  • What this means for you: the MMR vaccine is given in two doses at 12–15 months and 4–6 years. If you live in New York, check your children’s vaccination records now — vaccination itself still requires your consent, and the emergency runs through November 4.

A statewide emergency with no lockdowns

New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a statewide disaster emergency on Monday in response to a fast-growing measles outbreak, the first such declaration by a US state since measles cases began surging in 2025. The emergency declaration imposes no lockdowns or restrictions on the general public. Instead, it temporarily widens the pool of health professionals authorized to administer measles vaccines and conduct or order testing, allowing the state to respond more quickly in communities where infections are appearing.

https://x.com/MarioNawfal/status/2107304853714444532

"After reviewing the latest data on measles cases in New York State, I am declaring a State Disaster Emergency to strengthen our ongoing efforts to confront this disease," Hochul said in a statement. "No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease."

Otsego County in Central New York has recorded the most cases of any county in the state, with 20 infections since January, according to the New York Post. Local health departments have administered more than 1,000 MMR doses in rural areas since July 15.

Why measles is back

Measles was declared eliminated in the United States in 2000. For the quarter century that followed, the country averaged just 180 measles cases a year, according to federal data. But the disease began an historic resurgence in 2025, and 2026 is now the worst US measles year since 1991, with nearly 3,900 cases reported nationwide, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

New York’s outbreak is not the largest the country has seen in the past two years. At least 762 cases were associated with an outbreak in West Texas last year, and an outbreak in South Carolina reached nearly 1,000 cases before it was declared over in April. The most immediate concern for New York is next door: Pennsylvania is battling a fast-spreading outbreak with 977 cases and five deaths as of October 2, mostly in rural counties that border New York, the executive order said. Pennsylvania health officials said on Monday the state’s total had passed 1,000 cases, making it the largest state outbreak in more than three decades.

What changes under the order

The executive order expands the pool of people eligible to administer the MMR (measles, mumps and rubella) vaccine to paramedics, advanced EMS providers, pharmacists and midwives, in addition to physicians. Registered nurses can now order tests for suspected measles without waiting for a physician, and pharmacists can vaccinate children as young as two. The state is also providing epidemiological support to investigate cases, conduct contact tracing and expedite laboratory testing.

All MMR vaccinations must now be reported to New York state or New York City immunization registries within 72 hours, with the order waiving adults’ consent for such reporting. Vaccination itself still requires the consent of the patient or a legal guardian. The emergency took effect on Monday and runs through November 4.

What families should do now

The outbreak is concentrated in under-immunized rural communities, and the Indian diaspora has a large presence in New York and New Jersey — many families moved to suburban and upstate counties where some of these cases are appearing. The measles vaccine schedule is standard across the US and India alike: two doses of MMR, the first at 12–15 months and the second at 4–6 years, with the two-dose series about 97% effective at preventing the disease.

Parents who are unsure whether their children are fully vaccinated can check immunization records through their pediatrician or, now, the state registry. symptoms — high fever, cough, runny nose and a characteristic rash — typically appear 7–14 days after exposure. Anyone experiencing symptoms should call ahead before visiting a clinic or emergency room so staff can isolate the patient and prevent waiting-room spread.

What to watch next

The emergency declaration expires November 4 unless renewed, so health officials have a four-week window to push vaccination into the hardest-hit communities before winter, when indoor gathering season makes respiratory viruses spread faster. The critical indicator will be whether case counts in the 18 affected counties level off and whether the Pennsylvania outbreak spills further across the border.

New York’s governor declared a statewide disaster emergency on October 5 as measles cases spread across 18 rural counties.
nri_angle: Indian-American families in New York and New Jersey, many in the suburban and upstate counties hit by the outbreak, should check their children's two-dose MMR vaccination records as the state pushes an emergency vaccination drive through November 4.
